title: How would you design a system like Uber (actors, services, DB design, real-time location, matching engine, scaling, communication, security, monitoring)?
shortTitle: How would you design a system like Uber
topicTitle: How would you design a system like Uber

s1_definition.profdef: Designing a ride-hailing system like Uber means decomposing it into clear actors (rider, driver, admin), a set of focused microservices (user, trip, location, matching, pricing, payment, notification), a data model split by service, a real-time location pipeline that ingests frequent driver GPS updates and indexes them geospatially, a matching engine that finds the nearest suitable driver using geospatial queries and dispatches an offer, and the cross-cutting concerns of horizontal scaling, synchronous and asynchronous communication, authentication and authorization, and end-to-end observability. The hardest parts are the high-write real-time location stream and the low-latency matching, which drive the choice of a geospatial index, a fast in-memory store, and event-driven communication.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of it like National Bank of India running a fleet of mobile cash vans. Customers (riders) request a van, van drivers constantly radio in their location, a dispatcher (the matching engine) keeps a live map of where every van is and assigns the nearest free one to each request, a pricing desk calculates the fare, and the payment desk, which is exactly the bank's transfer logic, moves money from the customer to the driver and takes the bank's commission. The dispatcher must answer "who is nearest?" in a fraction of a second even with thousands of vans reporting their position every few seconds, so you keep a fast live map rather than asking a slow central ledger each time.
s1_definition.oneliner: Design Uber as focused microservices around a real-time geospatial location pipeline and a low-latency matching engine, with event-driven communication, a fast in-memory geo-index for "who is nearest", a payment service that moves money safely, and full observability, all scaled horizontally.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Designing a ride-hailing system like Uber means decomposing it into clear actors (rider, driver, admin), a set of focused microservices (user, trip, location, matching, pricing, payment, notification), a data model split by service, a real-time location pipeline that ingests frequent driver GPS updates and indexes them geospatially, a matching engine that finds the nearest suitable driver using geospatial queries and dispatches an offer, and the cross-cutting concerns of horizontal scaling, synchronous and asynchronous communication, authentication and authorization, and end-to-end observability. The hardest parts are the high-write real-time location stream and the low-latency matching, which drive the choice of a geospatial index, a fast in-memory store, and event-driven communication.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of it like National Bank of India running a fleet of mobile cash vans. Customers (riders) request a van, van drivers constantly radio in their location, a dispatcher (the matching engine) keeps a live map of where every van is and assigns the nearest free one to each request, a pricing desk calculates the fare, and the payment desk, which is exactly the bank's transfer logic, moves money from the customer to the driver and takes the bank's commission. The dispatcher must answer "who is nearest?" in a fraction of a second even with thousands of vans reporting their position every few seconds, so you keep a fast live map rather than asking a slow central ledger each time.

**One line to remember:** Design Uber as focused microservices around a real-time geospatial location pipeline and a low-latency matching engine, with event-driven communication, a fast in-memory geo-index for "who is nearest", a payment service that moves money safely, and full observability, all scaled horizontally.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with the actors and the core use cases, because they define the services. The actors are the rider, who requests and takes trips and pays, the driver, who goes online, receives trip offers, drives, and gets paid, and the admin or operations staff, who monitor and intervene. The core flows are: driver goes online and streams location; rider requests a ride from pickup to drop; the system matches a nearby driver; the trip runs with live tracking; the fare is computed and charged; and both parties are notified and rated.

Decompose into microservices, each owning its data. A User/Auth service manages rider and driver profiles and issues tokens. A Driver/Location service ingests the high-frequency GPS stream and maintains current driver positions and availability. A Trip service owns the lifecycle of a trip from requested to completed. A Matching/Dispatch service finds and offers drivers. A Pricing service computes fares including surge. A Payment service charges the rider and settles the driver, which is where the bank's money-movement logic lives. A Notification service pushes updates to phones. A Ratings service records feedback. Each service has its own database following database-per-service, so the location service can use a store optimised for geo while the payment service uses a strongly consistent relational database.

Real-time location is the defining challenge. Drivers send their GPS coordinates every few seconds, so with many drivers this is a very high write rate of small updates. You do not write each ping into a relational table; instead the location service consumes the pings, usually through a message stream, and keeps each driver's current position in a fast in-memory store with a geospatial index, for example Redis with its geo commands or a specialised geo index. The index supports "find all drivers within radius R of this point" quickly. You also keep only the latest position per driver for matching, while optionally streaming the raw trail to cheaper storage for analytics and dispute resolution. Partitioning the location data by geographic region, often with a geohash or an S2/H3 cell as the key, keeps each shard's working set bounded and makes nearby-driver queries local.

The matching engine turns a request into an assigned driver with low latency. When a rider requests a trip at a pickup point, the matching service queries the geo index for candidate drivers near the pickup, filters by availability, vehicle type, rating, and direction, ranks them by estimated time of arrival, and sends a trip offer to the best candidate. If the driver declines or times out, it offers the next, which is why the offer loop must be fast and stateful per request. Matching is latency-critical, so it reads from the in-memory geo store, not a disk database, and it must avoid double-assigning a driver, which it does with an atomic claim on the driver's availability, for example a compare-and-set in the fast store or a short lock, so two concurrent requests cannot grab the same driver.

Database design follows the services. The trip database is relational, storing trips with status, rider, driver, pickup, drop, timestamps, and fare, because trips need transactions and strong consistency. The payment database is relational and strongly consistent, recording charges and driver payouts with idempotency keys. The user database holds profiles. The location "database" is really the in-memory geo store for current positions plus a time-series or object store for historical trails. You keep geospatial and high-write data out of the transactional relational databases to protect their performance.

Communication is a deliberate mix. Synchronous REST or gRPC is used where an immediate answer is needed, for example the rider app asking the trip service to create a trip, or matching asking pricing for a fare estimate. Asynchronous events over a stream like Kafka are used for everything that can be eventual and high-volume: location pings, trip-state changes that fan out to notifications and analytics, and payment events. Event-driven communication decouples the services and smooths the enormous location write load. Live trip tracking to the rider's phone typically uses a persistent connection such as WebSocket or a push channel, fed by the location stream.

Scaling is horizontal and shard-aware. Stateless services like trip, pricing, and matching scale by adding instances behind a load balancer. The location pipeline scales by partitioning the stream and the geo store by region, so a city's load stays within its shards and a hot city does not overwhelm a quiet one. The in-memory geo store is clustered and partitioned by geo cell. You cache hot read data like driver profiles and fare rules. Capacity is planned from peak, for example rush-hour surges, with headroom so losing a node does not cascade.

Security and monitoring are non-negotiable, especially because money moves. Authentication uses tokens, with riders and drivers getting scoped access, and the API gateway validates every request, rate-limits, and terminates TLS, while service-to-service traffic uses mTLS. Authorization ensures a rider can only see their own trips and a driver only their own offers. Sensitive data like payment details is encrypted and handled by the payment service alone. Observability includes metrics on match latency, trip success rate, and payment failures, structured logs keyed by a trip correlation id, and distributed tracing so a single trip's journey across services is visible, with alerts on match latency and payment error spikes.

Senior nuances worth stating: keep the matching read path entirely in memory and make driver claims atomic to prevent double assignment; partition everything geographically so load and failures stay local; use the outbox pattern and idempotency in the payment path so a retry never double-charges a rider; separate the current-position store from the historical trail store because their access patterns differ sharply; and design surge pricing as its own service reading demand and supply signals so it can evolve without touching matching. The whole design is an exercise in isolating the high-write real-time component from the strongly-consistent money component.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs a fleet of mobile cash-delivery vans, and customers like Rajesh request a van to their location. Each van radios its GPS position every few seconds, which is a huge stream of tiny updates, and writing each one into the core banking ledger would overwhelm it. This is exactly the real-time location problem, solved by keeping current van positions in a fast in-memory geo index rather than the transactional database.

Problem 2 — When Rajesh requests a van, the system must instantly find the nearest free van, and two customers must never be assigned the same van. This is exactly the matching-engine problem, solved by a geospatial radius query over the in-memory index plus an atomic claim on the van's availability so it cannot be double-assigned.

Problem 3 — After the delivery, money must move from Rajesh to the driver's account with the bank's commission deducted, exactly once even if the request is retried. This is exactly the payment problem, solved by the bank's transfer logic with an idempotency key.

Our mini-project builds a compact dispatch core. The code keeps van positions in an in-memory geo store, runs a nearest-available matching query with an atomic claim, and then settles payment from the customer to the driver with an idempotency key and a commission split. The demo matches a van for Rajesh and settles the fare, using Priya's account as the destination for a second request.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three vans streaming their positions, and Rajesh requesting a van at pickup point latitude 28.6145, longitude 77.2085, with a fare of four hundred fifty rupees.

Step 1: Each van sends its current GPS position, and the location service writes only the latest position per van into the in-memory geo index. No position touches the transactional database; the geo index is the fast store that makes nearby queries quick.

Step 2: Rajesh requests a ride. The matching engine queries the geo index for available vans within three kilometres of his pickup. VAN-01 and VAN-02 are nearby and available; VAN-03 is far and excluded. The engine ranks by distance and picks the nearest, VAN-01.

Step 3: The engine atomically claims VAN-01. The claim succeeds, so VAN-01 is now marked unavailable in the fast store. This atomic claim is what prevents a second rider from being assigned the same van.

Step 4: A trip is created from Rajesh (SAV2001) to driver VAN-01 with a fare of four hundred fifty rupees, recorded in the trip database with status assigned, then in progress, then completed as the delivery runs.

Step 5: On completion the payment service settles the fare with idempotency key idem-TRIP-1001. It computes the bank's twenty percent commission, ninety rupees, and the driver payout, three hundred sixty rupees, then debits Rajesh and credits the driver and the bank's commission account in one transaction.

Step 6: The settlement is retried with the same idempotency key, and the payment service sees the key already processed and ignores it, so Rajesh is charged exactly once. This is the exactly-once money guarantee.

Step 7: Priya then requests a van near the same point. The matching engine queries the geo index, but VAN-01 is claimed, so it is filtered out and Priya is matched to VAN-02 instead, proving no double assignment occurred.

Final output:

```
2026-10-24 15:11:20 INFO    claimed VAN-01
2026-10-24 15:11:20 INFO    Rajesh matched to VAN-01 within 3.0km
2026-10-24 15:11:20 INFO    SETTLE TRIP-1001: debit SAV2001 Rs.450 → driver VAN-01 Rs.360, bank commission Rs.90
2026-10-24 15:11:20 WARNING duplicate settlement ignored for idem-TRIP-1001
2026-10-24 15:11:20 INFO    claimed VAN-02
2026-10-24 15:11:20 INFO    Priya matched to VAN-02 (never the same claimed van)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To design a system like Uber I start from the actors and use cases, then decompose into focused microservices, each owning its own data. The actors are rider, driver, and operations staff, and the services are user and auth, a location service for the driver GPS stream, a matching and dispatch service, a trip service for the trip lifecycle, a pricing service including surge, a payment service that moves money, and notification and ratings services. Database-per-service lets the location service use a store optimised for geography while the payment service uses a strongly consistent relational database.

The defining challenge is real-time location, because drivers send GPS pings every few seconds and that is an enormous stream of tiny writes. I never write each ping into a relational table; the location service consumes the pings, usually through a stream, and keeps only each driver's latest position in a fast in-memory geospatial store like Redis geo, partitioned by region using a geohash or cell so a busy city stays within its own shards, while raw trails go to cheaper storage for analytics and disputes. The matching engine is latency-critical, so it reads candidate drivers from that in-memory index within a radius of the pickup, filters by availability, vehicle type, and rating, ranks by estimated arrival, and offers the best driver, expanding the radius if none is found. Crucially it claims the chosen driver atomically with a compare-and-set in the fast store so two riders can never be assigned the same driver.

Communication is a deliberate mix: synchronous REST or gRPC where an immediate answer is needed, like creating a trip or getting a fare estimate, and asynchronous events over Kafka for everything high-volume or eventual, like location pings and trip-state changes that fan out to notifications and analytics, with live tracking pushed to the phone over a WebSocket. Scaling is horizontal for the stateless services and shard-aware for the location pipeline and geo store, planned from peak with headroom. Security runs through the gateway with token validation, rate limiting, and TLS, mTLS between services, strict authorization so a rider sees only their own trips, and encryption of payment data, and observability covers match-latency metrics, trip success rate, payment error rate, per-trip tracing, and alerting.

I frame this to an interviewer as banking's own problem: at National Bank of India we modelled a mobile cash-van fleet exactly this way. Vans streamed GPS into an in-memory geo index, a matching engine answered who is nearest in milliseconds with an atomic claim so two customers never got the same van, and settlement used the bank's transfer logic with an idempotency key so a retried payment never double-charged the customer, splitting the fare into the driver payout and the bank's commission. The single biggest design lesson was to isolate the high-write real-time component, which lives entirely in a fast in-memory geo store, from the strongly consistent money component, which lives in a relational database with idempotency and the outbox pattern, because mixing them would either overwhelm the ledger or make matching too slow.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I design Uber as focused, data-owning microservices around a geographically partitioned in-memory geo index for real-time location, a low-latency matching engine that claims drivers atomically to avoid double assignment, event-driven communication for high-volume flows, a safe idempotent payment service for the money, and full observability, with the whole thing scaled horizontally and partitioned by region.
